explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The people of Jerusalem went into exile in the fifth month of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the king of Judah named last in the list (Jeremiah 1:3). That's where the stretch of Jeremiah's messages ends. The word of the LORD kept coming to him through the days of Jehoiakim and on until that point.

Close to the right neighborhood, but not what verse 3 says. It says the people of Jerusalem went into exile. Walls do come up later in this passage, and not for building. The kings from the north attack them (Jeremiah 1:15).
Kings are all over this verse, friend. Jehoiakim and Zedekiah get named, both sons of Josiah. But the verse doesn't say anything about a crowning. It says the people of Jerusalem went into exile.
That's the one. The LORD says, "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you…" (Jeremiah 1:5). Think about that, baker. Before Jeremiah had a first day, the LORD already knew him.

Dust does show up in the Bible when the LORD formed the first man from it (Genesis 2:7). Here, though, the LORD says He formed Jeremiah in the womb. And He says He knew him before that. I like that this verse starts before the beginning.
Gardens are in the Bible, like the one in Eden (Genesis 2:8). But the LORD's words to Jeremiah are about the womb. He says He knew him there, and even before it. No dirt on this one.

Right, baker. The LORD says, "…before you were born I set you apart and appointed you as a prophet to the nations." So the appointing came before Jeremiah's birth. His job was picked before he could pick anything.

Kings are in the passage, but the LORD doesn't appoint Jeremiah as one. Josiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah are named as kings of Judah in the days when the word of the LORD came to him (Jeremiah 1:2-3). Jeremiah himself is a priest's son from Anathoth (Jeremiah 1:1). The LORD appoints him as a prophet.

Judge is a fair guess, friend, since the Bible has judges. But the title in verse 5 is prophet, and the LORD appoints Jeremiah as a prophet to the nations. I'd have squinted at that name tag twice myself.
Yes, friend. Jeremiah says, "I surely do not know how to speak, for I am only a child!" The LORD has just appointed him as a prophet to the nations. I think speaking was exactly what was on his mind.
Lead is a natural guess, since Jeremiah is getting a big assignment. But Jeremiah's words are, "I surely do not know how to speak…" The job is about words. Nothing in his answer is about leading.
Fighting does come up later, but Jeremiah isn't the one saying it. In verse 19 the LORD says they will fight against him. Jeremiah's own worry here is that he doesn't know how to speak.

I get why you'd think so, friend, but it's False. The LORD says, "…to everyone I send you, you must go, and all that I command you, you must speak." That's all of it. No picking and choosing from the list.
Right, baker. The LORD says, "…to everyone I send you, you must go, and all that I command you, you must speak." He says everyone and all. Jeremiah doesn't get to cross anything off.
That's it. The LORD says, "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you…" Notice the reason is not that the people are friendly. The reason is that the LORD is with Jeremiah.
Not the word the LORD picks here. He says, "Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you…" The reason for not being afraid is that He's with Jeremiah. Deliver is the word to hold onto.
That isn't the word in verse 8, friend. The LORD says He is with Jeremiah "to deliver" him. That's a promise to bring him through, and it comes with "Do not be afraid…"
Yes, baker! The LORD says, "Behold, I have put My words in your mouth." The mouth Jeremiah was worried about now has the LORD's words in it. I'd say that settles the speaking question.

A new song is a real Bible thing, like in Psalm 40:3, where the psalmist says the LORD put a new song in his mouth. But here the LORD says what He puts in Jeremiah's mouth is His words. Same spot, different gift.

You're remembering another prophet there. In Isaiah 6:6-7, a seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with a burning coal. Isaiah was a prophet too. For Jeremiah, the LORD touches his mouth Himself and says He has put His words there.
Yes, friend. The list ends with "…to build and plant." So the job has four hard verbs up front, then two more at the end. The LORD's list doesn't stop at tearing down.

It's True, baker. The LORD's list says "…to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant." Building and planting are right there at the end. Easy to miss when the first four verbs hit so hard.
That's right. The LORD says, "You have observed correctly…" Jeremiah saw a branch of an almond tree, and he saw it right. I'd bet he breathed out after that one.
This one is True. The LORD says, "You have observed correctly…" Jeremiah saw a branch of an almond tree (Jeremiah 1:11), and the LORD confirms he saw it right.

explanations.answer: His word to make it happen
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, "…I am watching over My word to accomplish it." So His word is what He keeps His eye on. He says this right after Jeremiah tells Him he sees a branch of an almond tree (Jeremiah 1:11).
That sounds comforting, but it isn't what the LORD says here. He says, "…I am watching over My word to accomplish it." The thing He's watching over is His word.
The land is in the passage, but not in this verse. In verse 12 the LORD says He is watching over His word to accomplish it. That's the thing He names, friend.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land." That's what the tilting pot was showing. It's a heavy word.
That's a kinder word than the one in the verse. The LORD says, "Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land." It's a heavy part of the passage.
Mercy is a good word, friend, but it's not what the LORD names here. He says, "Disaster from the north will be poured out on all who live in the land." It's a hard thing for Jeremiah to hear.

Right. The LORD says the kings "…will come and set up their thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem." Thrones is the word the verse picks. Verse 15 goes on to say they will attack all her surrounding walls and all the other cities of Judah.

Tents are what you'd expect from an army, friend, but the verse picks a different word. The LORD says the kings will set up their thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem. They aren't just passing through.

Burning incense to other gods comes up in verse 16, but that's a different verse. Verse 15 is the one about the northern kings. It says they set up their thrones at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: They left Him for other gods
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says He will pronounce His judgments "…because they have forsaken Me…" That's the reason He gives in verse 16. He adds that they burned incense to other gods and worshiped the works of their own hands.

explanations.answer: They made a treaty with Egypt
explanations.explanation: A treaty might sound like a good reason, but it isn't in these verses. The LORD gives His own reason in verse 16: "…they have forsaken Me…" Then He adds that they burned incense to other gods.

explanations.answer: They let the temple fall into ruins
explanations.explanation: That one isn't in this passage, friend. The LORD says it's because they have forsaken Him and burned incense to other gods. He also says they worshiped the works of their own hands.

That's the one. The LORD says, "Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them." Right before that, Jeremiah is told to get ready, stand up and tell them everything the LORD commands (Jeremiah 1:17).
Distracted is a close cousin, but the LORD uses a stronger word. He says, "Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them." It's about being scared off by the people.
The LORD does say to get ready and stand up, so I see how you got there. But the word in verse 17 is intimidated. He says, "Do not be intimidated by them, or I will terrify you before them."

explanations.answer: The whole land and its leaders
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says it's "…against the whole land…" and then He lists them: the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land. That's a long list to stand against. The LORD says He has made Jeremiah like a fortified city, an iron pillar, and bronze walls.

The armies from the north are in the passage, but they aren't in this list. In verse 18 the LORD says against "…the whole land…" Then He names the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
Egypt isn't mentioned anywhere in this chapter, friend. The LORD says the walls are against the whole land. He lists the kings of Judah, its officials, its priests, and the people of the land.
That's a nice thought, but the LORD says it differently. He says, "They will fight against you but will never overcome you…" So the fight is coming. What the LORD promises is that they won't win.
Right, baker. The LORD says, "They will fight against you but will never overcome you, since I am with you to deliver you…" The fighting happens. The promise is that Jeremiah won't be overcome.
